title: The three lines: right, left, and the middle line that reaches the inner Keser
overview:
In *Tikun* the *sefiros* stand as a *partzuf* in three lines. On the right, *chachma*, *chesed* and *netzach*: *chachma* looks past the outside to what it stands for, "it's the thought that counts", and so leans to kindness. On the left, *bina*, *gevura* and *hod*: *bina* looks at the outside, draws distinctions, and is nitpicky. Each branch is separate from its source, which is why a high-minded idea loses force by the time it has to go out knocking on doors in the cold.

The two sides come together only through the middle line. *Daas* sees both as tools and makes a judgment call for this person, a human thing no computer can do; *tiferes* is mercy after the verdict, Yaakov's way of giving a ladder out of the mud; *yesod* decides between *netzach* and *hod*, the kidneys that say yes and no. The middle line can join them because it reaches the inner *Keser*, the will with no reason, all or nothing. The *paroches* is where that will takes a form, so prayer goes before it to change judgement to kindness.

terms.gloss: lines: the three lines of a partzuf, chachma, chesed and netzach on the right, bina, gevura and hod on the left, daas, tiferes and yesod in the middle
the Keser within the Keser: the inner, essential will, which does not split into lines
acknowledgement: holding back, caution, giving up one's strength before what is bigger
the daas that tilts: it sees both sides and decides how much of each, for this person and this situation
mercy: it comes after the verdict, and lets the person off because the goal is that he improve
the kidneys that advise: netzach and hod, which say yes and no on how to carry out a decision
the weighing of the mind: the whole middle line, which makes a judgment call
the middle bar: the pole through all the boards of the Mishkan; the middle line, one through every level
the hidden reason for the will: chachma of Keser, hidden because the will covers it, and really a taste of delight
the days of old: the middos of the will and delight, the original dream before it is brought down to what is possible
the curtain between the Holy and the Holy of Holies: the screen between the essential will and the will that has a form
the membrane of air, which he calls the arachnoid membrane: the screen through which the essential delight reaches the faculties

sections.title: Three lines: the inner Keser does not divide, its outer side does
sections.summary: In *Tikun* the *sefiros* stand as a *partzuf* (a stature) in three lines, right, left and middle. The inner *Keser*, the essential will, does not split into lines; from its outer side, already *chachma* of *Keser*, they divide.

phrases.he: (כא) ובזה יובן כללות ענין ההתכללות דג' קוין דנאצלים,
חח''ן מימין ובג''ה משמאל ודת''י באמצע כו'
phrases.en: that when the *sefiros* go out, *chachma*, *chesed*, *netzach* is on the right, *bina*, *gevura*, *hod* is on the left, and then *daas*, *tiferes*, *yesod* stays in the middle.

blocks.text: Now the three *kavin* (lines). In *Tohu* (the world of Chaos) the *sefiros* (Divine attributes) are separate *nekudos* (points); in *Tikun* (repair) they become a *partzuf* (lit. face; a full stature), which means three lines: *chachma* (wisdom), *chesed* (kindness) and *netzach* (victory) on the right; *bina* (understanding), *gevura* (might, restraint) and *hod* (acknowledgement) on the left; *daas* (knowledge), *tiferes* (beauty) and *yesod* (foundation) in the middle.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב בפרדס דפנימית הכתר הנקרא כתר שבכתר,
לא נחלק לג' קוין
phrases.en: That doesn't split up into three *kavin*.

phrases.he: בחינת חיצוניות שבו,
phrases.en: but from the *chitzoniyus* of the *ratzon* already,

phrases.he: ממנו מתחלק לג' קוין
והוא מבחינת חכמה שבכתר כו', וכידוע בכונות דהגדול הגבור והנורא כו'.

blocks.text: As the *Pardes* says, the *pnimiyus* (inner side) of *Keser*, the *Keser sheb'Keser*, is the inner *ratzon* (will) itself, the *nekuda*, the *etzem* (essence) of what you want, and does not split into lines. From the *chitzoniyus* (outer side) of the will it divides into a *partzuf* in *yosher* (the straight line), as with *Arich Anpin*: *Chabad* and the six *middos* (emotional attributes).

This is from *chachma* of *Keser*, as known from the *kavanos* (intentions) of "the great, the mighty and the awesome," the three lines in *Keser*: great is *chesed*, mighty is *gevura*, and the *heh*, "the," is in a way a *hispashtus* (spreading forth).

sections.title: The right line and the left: chachma looks past the form, bina at it
sections.summary: On the right, *chesed* is a branch of *chachma* and *netzach* a branch of *chesed*, each separate from its source; on the left, *bina*, *gevura* and *hod* are the opposite. *Chachma* looks past the outside to what it stands for and so leans to kindness; *bina* looks at the outside, makes distinctions and leans to judgement.

phrases.he: וביאור הדברים, הנה בחינת התכללות הקוין ימין ושמאל הוא על ידי קו האמצעי דוקא
phrases.en: The right and the left lines are connected through the middle line.

blocks.text: The right and left lines are included in each other, and connected at all, *davka* through the middle line.

phrases.he: והענין הוא דקו הימין חח''ן, הרי החסד ענף החכמה ומובדל הימנה
phrases.en: On the right line, *chesed* is a branch of *chachma*, but it's separate from it.

phrases.he: והוא מה שנסתעף החסד מצד השכל והטעם, שמטה כלפי חסד
phrases.en: This is when, because of a reason, you lean towards *chesed*.

phrases.he: בדבר מורכב כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: On the right, **chesed is a branch of chachma, but it's separate from it**: **because of a reason, you lean towards chesed**. It is not an *etzem chesed* (essential kindness); your *sechel* (intellect) causes it.

blocks.title: The right hand gives
blocks.text: The right arm is on the same side as the right side of the brain, and you usually take and give with your right hand: one reason the right hand is a *mashal* (analogy) for *chesed*, on *chachma*'s side.
*Chachma* looks past the form, at the abstract thing it stands for; *bina* looks at the outer form. So *chachma* leans towards *chesed*, and *bina* towards *gevura*.

blocks.title: It's the thought that counts
blocks.text: Someone gives you a gift, and you look into it and say, "It's the thought that counts": that is *chachma*, looking deeper, at what it represents, and appreciating it very much.

blocks.title: Looking past a person's deeds
blocks.text: So with a person who outwardly is not so good: you look past what he does, at his inner motivation, a person like you, really just misguided, and you can relate to him. That is *chachma*.

*Bina* focuses on the outside, and there no gift will ever properly express the love behind it: be *medakdek* (exacting) about the outside and you always find the flaw. So with a person, *ein tzaddik ba'aretz* (there is no righteous man on earth): be exacting about how his actions live up to what you could expect, and you will always find something wrong.

You can look at it either way. *Chachma* says the feeling can never be shown properly outside, so look past it: the *etzem* connection is there, and how it is expressed does not really matter.

*Bina* looks at the outside and insists that it come out: make the effort to express what you mean, act in a way befitting who you are and our relationship. It is very nitpicky. So *chachma* leans towards *chesed*.

blocks.title: The poor person
blocks.text: Looking at a poor man from the side of *chachma*, a person finds common ground, relates to him and sympathizes, and so wants to give him *tzedaka* (charity); or he understands intellectually that it is good to be nice to him.

phrases.he: וכן הנצח ענף החסד,
phrases.en: and likewise, *netzach* is an *anaf* of *chesed*,

phrases.he: מובדל הימנו.
phrases.en: but it's also separate from the *chesed*.

phrases.he: דהיינו מצד החסד יחויב בחינת הניצוח להביא החסד למעשה בפועל ממש כו'

blocks.text: Likewise *netzach* is an *anaf* (branch) of *chesed*, and separate from it. *Chesed* is *hispashtus*, wanting to give; but giving anything in deed meets opposition, and you have to figure out how to do it. That is *netzach*, which *chesed* needs to reach the deed.

blocks.title: The father teaching his son
blocks.text: You always have to fight the *kli* (vessel), as in *Tanya*'s *mashal* of a father teaching his son. Out of *chesed* he wants to give his son his *chachma*, but he must bring it down to the son's level. *Netzach* is the work of crossing the language barrier and the different backgrounds, to bring it across in a way the other will appreciate.

blocks.title: Running after him to help
blocks.text: The simple case is the right leg. Wanting to do a man *chesed* obliges you even to run after him to help him, which is really *netzach*; and if there is an obstacle, the *chesed* says you should even be willing to fight for what's right.

But the right and left lines are detached. So a person can be very high-minded in his *chachma*, less enthusiastic in his emotion, and much less in *netzach*, actually running after someone. Still it obliges him.

blocks.title: Mivtzaim in the cold
blocks.text: Like *mivtzaim* (outreach campaigns). *Chachma* sees that it is right to help other Jews, and he feels a *chesed*. Actually doing it, raising money, finding the time and the people, going out in the cold knocking on doors with menorahs, uncomfortable for many, is *netzach*. The *chesed* obliges it, but being detached, it loses some of its *koach* (power).

phrases.he: וקו השמאל היפוכו,
phrases.en: the left line is the opposite of everything in the right line,

phrases.he: כמו שכל המטה כלפי דין שנסתעף הימנו מידת הדין כו'
כך בינה גבורה כו'
phrases.en: So too is *bina gevura*, that *bina* leans towards *gevura*,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב אני בינה, לי גבורה כו'
phrases.en: I am *bina* and *gevura* is mine,

phrases.he: דהחכמה נוטה לחסדים
ובינה מינה דינין כו'
phrases.en: that from *bina* comes out *dinin*.

phrases.he: (וכמו שכתוב בעץ חיים דאבא מקור החסדים
phrases.en: that *Abba*'s the source of the *chassadim*.

phrases.he: ואימא מקור כל הגבורות כו' וכידוע)
phrases.en: and *Ima* is the *makor* of all the *gevuros*

blocks.text: The left line is the opposite: an intellect that leans towards *din* (judgement), from which judgement branches out. So *bina* leans towards *gevura*, as it says, "I am *bina*, *gevura* is mine": *chachma* leans to the *chassadim* (kindnesses), and from *bina* come the *dinin* (judgements).

As *Etz Chaim* says, *Abba* is the source of the *chassadim*. *Chachma* grasps the *mahus* (what a thing is), the abstract, and so always brings *chassadim*: it sees how something applies to everything and connects. Its nature is to break barriers and go deeper, to the essence, which has no bounds.

*Bina* is the opposite: to define, compartmentalize, draw sharp distinctions. To speak you need *bina*, to find the exact words; to understand a speaker you also need *chachma*, to read between the lines for what he really means. You need both.

blocks.title: Living the story
blocks.text: Take a person reading. Knowing what the words literally mean is *bina*. When he no longer realizes he is reading, as if living the story, that is *chachma*: the words become transparent. That is the *pnimiyus* of the *mochin* (intellectual faculties), *mamash* (actually) one with its subject.

And *Ima* is the source of all the *gevuros*, because *bina* makes distinctions and breaks things up. It looks at the *chitzoniyus*, the *gilui* (revelation), not the *etzem*, which is itself limited, the *inyan* of *gevuros*; and it cuts things up, letting a part stand for the whole, like the five *gevuros*, the final letters *mem*, *nun*, *tzadi*, *peh*, *chaf*, to be discussed later.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 78 opens by finishing line 12, which class 77 ended in the middle of.

sections.title: The middle line: daas sees both sides and makes a judgment call
sections.summary: Two ways of looking at anything, past the outside or at it, come together only through *daas*. *Daas* holds both as tools and decides, for this person and this situation, how much of each: a human, subjective judgment no computer can make.

phrases.he: ובחינת ההתכללות דב' קוין הללו שיבואו להתחבר במקום א',
הוא על ידי קו האמצעי דת''י כו'
phrases.en: it's *davka* the middle thing, which is *daas*.

blocks.question: How can *chachma* and *bina*, or *chesed* and *gevura*, come together?
blocks.text: Every situation has these two sides, one way of looking and the other. Which do you choose?

blocks.title: Avraham saw their inner good
blocks.text: You can look at people as Avraham did: he saw their inner good, a good desire badly expressed even when they did bad things, and valued their potential, overlooking their shortcomings. Or you can look with *bina*, at the outside. Neither really detracts from the other.
They are two totally different ways of looking, so having them together takes *davka* the middle thing, *daas*.

phrases.he: כמו הדעת שהוא בחינת ממוצע להטות משכל של חסד לשכל של דין, ונקרא דעת נוטה

blocks.text: *Daas* is the intermediary that tilts from an intellect of *chesed* to one of *din*: *daas noteh* (the *daas* that tilts). It recognizes both sides: the inner good and the thought that counts, as between a parent and child, and the discomfort at how the person is acting. *Daas* can be *sovel* (bear) both.

And it sees what is best for this person now: how to get him to see that his potential is always there, that he will never bring it out perfectly since nobody's perfect, and that he should still work to express it as best he can. It tailors which side to stress and how much. "So it's a judgment call."

*Daas* is *davka* personal, an opinion, a human thing: "You couldn't have a computer make a decision on the level of *daas*." *Chachma* and *bina* are technical; *daas* asks what our real goal is, sees both sides as tools, and takes whichever side, or mix, will work best. That is *daas noteh*.

phrases.he: (וכמו כי יצר לב כו'
phrases.en: like with the *Mabul*,

phrases.he: שנעשה שכל וטעם לזכות, אשר תחלה היה זה השכל עצמו נוטה כלפי חוב, כמו שכתוב וירא כי רבה רעת כו' וכהאי גוונא וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר)

blocks.text: Like "the inclination of the heart" at the *Mabul* (the Flood): the same fact, that man is born bad, served both sides. The intellect of *chesed* says it is not their fault if they sin; that of *gevura* says they are sinning, and that is bad. The same reason that first leaned to guilt, "And He saw that the evil of man was great," became a reason to acquit.
Everything can be looked at two ways, and you have to choose: that is *daas*, an opinion, a subjective thing.

phrases.he: ונמצא בדעת יחובר ב' שכליים הפכיים דחסד וגבורה להיות נוטה לחסד באופן זה ולדין באופן זה וכהאי גוונא, גם במקום אחד

blocks.text: So in *daas* the opposite intellects of *chesed* and *gevura* are joined, leaning to *chesed* in this and to *din* in that. Both are true: up to a point we overlook, past it we do not. A little thing, depending on the person and the situation, you let go; but you expect a certain effort to come out.

As we said about the *Kav* (the line of light): the teacher measures how much effort he will put out and how much he wants from the student, how far he comes down and how far the student must work to come up. That decision is *davka* *daas*.
Even in one situation it is not all or nothing: you can help a little and make him work a little, a compromise. The middle line is individual, a human thing.

sections.title: Tiferes is mercy after the verdict: the attribute of Yaakov
sections.summary: *Tiferes* decides between *chesed* and *gevura* as mercy does: it comes only after judgement, when the person is guilty, and lets him off because the goal is that he improve. That is Yaakov's attribute: give as much help as is needed until he can stand on his own.

phrases.he: וכך מדת התפארת מכריע בין חסד וגבורה
phrases.en: the same way that *tiferes*, which is like a thing of mercy, is an intermediary between *chesed* and *gevura*.

phrases.he: שהוא כמו הרחמים,
phrases.en: which that's like mercy,

phrases.he: שאינו אלא אחר מידת הדין,
phrases.en: that after a person is guilty, and there's a problem,

phrases.he: שעם כל זה רחמנות פוטרו,
והיא מדת יעקב כידוע
phrases.en: it's the *midda* of Yaakov,

blocks.text: So too **tiferes, which is like a thing of mercy, is an intermediary between chesed and gevura**. Mercy comes only after judgement, **after a person is guilty, and there's a problem**: you beg the mercy of the court after the verdict.

*Rachmanus* (mercy) recognizes some good in the person; with no hope, no good in him, you would feel only *gevura*. You see the good and see it being messed up, and still overlook it sometimes, because he needs the help. The real goal is to help him, not a judgment system: "it's not really about who's right. The point is to get the person to improve."

blocks.title: Tests, scores and three strikes
blocks.text: Say a teacher has tests and scores, or three strikes and you're out, so that the responsibility and the work are on the student. Say he worked hard and it didn't work out. *Din* says rules are rules: let people off and they won't work or learn. So sometimes you must be harsh *davka*, to make an example that inspires others.

blocks.title: The student below the level of the class
blocks.text: But in private, where nobody will know, you can especially let it go. Take someone far below the class. If he really wants to improve he won't care about his grade; as long as he is learning he is happy. A teacher who sees that perhaps shouldn't send him up, but surely shouldn't punish him for failing. That *rachmanus* is *davka* between *chesed* and *gevura*, a human, subjective thing from *daas*.
It is **the midda of Yaakov**: I see your potential and your good, and I see your problems. I will come down and give you as much help as you need, but the aim is that you go on your own.

blocks.title: A ladder out of the mud
blocks.text: Like giving a person a ladder: not pulling him out of the mud and leaving it there, but helping him pull himself out, with as much help as he needs, until he stands on his own. That is the way of Yaakov.

sections.title: Yesod between netzach and hod: the kidneys that advise yes and no
sections.summary: *Netzach* and *hod* are the counsel on how to carry a decision out: *netzach* says to give and be proactive, *hod* to hold back and be cautious, like the kidneys that advise yes and no. *Yesod* decides between them, after the first decision of *daas*.

phrases.he: וכן בחינת יסוד
phrases.en: also *yesod*,

phrases.he: ממוצע לכלול ב' הפכים דנצח והוד

blocks.title: Spoon-feeding the student, or holding back
blocks.text:
So too *yesod* includes the opposites *netzach* and *hod*. Say you are teaching. *Netzach*, wanting to get the idea across, does all the work: explains everything simply, lays it all out, leaves the student nothing to do. He will get it, but he will not rise or learn to think for himself; he will "just become dependent on a good teacher."

*Hod* wants him to work harder: it asks hard questions and holds some of the information back, above him, so that he wants to work for it.

phrases.he: שהוא ענין כליות יועצות
phrases.en: *netzach* and *hod* is like the kidneys that give advice,

phrases.he: הן ולאו
phrases.en: that they say yes and no.

phrases.he: קודם השפעת המשפיע
כשצריך להשפיע עצם המדות חסד וגבורה
phrases.en: then when you want to bring across *chesed* and *gevura*,

blocks.title: The kidney and the glands on top of it
blocks.text: *Netzach* and *hod* are *kelayos yo'atzos*, the kidneys that give advice, saying yes and no. Every organ the Torah talks about has three parts, for *Chabad*, *chagas* and *nehi* (the three triads of *sefiros*), and so, from what Rabbi Walters researched, does the kidney: what English calls the kidney is only the bottom third, and on top are two stacked adrenal glands, the top one tied to the pituitary gland, working with the brain to regulate the body.

sensitivity.reason: Describes the adrenal glands as two glands stacked on the kidney, the top one tied to the pituitary, as anatomy from his own research; loose as medicine, and a reader may take it as fact.
sensitivity.publishable: *Netzach* and *hod* are *kelayos yo'atzos*, the kidneys that give advice, saying yes and no. Every organ the Torah talks about has three parts, for *Chabad*, *chagas* and *nehi* (the three triads of *sefiros*), and so does the kidney.
sensitivity.judgmentNote: Close to standard anatomy (the adrenal glands sit on the kidney, and the adrenal cortex is regulated by the pituitary), offered as his own research to explain kelayos yo'atzos; weigh whether it can print as he gave it.

blocks.title: Adrenaline and testosterone
blocks.text:
The middle gland answers not to the brain but to the emotions. It gives off adrenaline, a *hod* response: scared, facing something bigger than him, a person goes into fight or flight; he gives up hope and so will give all his *koach* away, and *hod* is like *mesirus nefesh* (self-sacrifice).

It also secretes testosterone, a thing of *netzach*, confidence: that is why teenage boys, high in testosterone, are cocky, unafraid of danger and always doing crazy stuff, pumped up to take on anything.

sensitivity.reason: Assigns adrenaline and testosterone to two stacked adrenal glands and ties them to hod and netzach as physiology; loose as medicine, and a reader may take it as fact.
sensitivity.publishable:
Fear brings a *hod* response: scared, facing something bigger than him, a person goes into fight or flight; he gives up hope and so will give all his *koach* away, and *hod* is like *mesirus nefesh* (self-sacrifice).

Confidence is a thing of *netzach*: a teenager unafraid of danger and always doing crazy stuff, pumped up to take on anything.
sensitivity.judgmentNote: Adrenaline and adrenal androgens do come from the adrenal glands, though not from two stacked glands as he describes; weigh whether his physiology of hod and netzach can print with his own hedge, or only its point.

blocks.text: The kidney itself strains the blood, good from bad, on the level of *nehi*, as the digestive system is like *netzach* and *hod*: *netzach* says yes, to give; *hod* says no, to hold back.

Before the giver gives, **when you want to bring across chesed and gevura**: say you have found someone guilty, a verdict without a sentence. What do we do with him? Or you decided something is a problem: how do we get rid of it? *Netzach* and *hod* work out an *eitza* (counsel).

One counsels acting boldly: *netzach*. *Hod* is reserved and cautious, sometimes a healthy respect, like a *hoda'a* (acknowledgement) that a gun is dangerous; but someone with anxiety has too much *hod*, and that is not good.

blocks.title: The zealots in the time of the Beis HaMikdash
blocks.text: And sometimes there is too much *netzach*: the *Biryonim* (zealots) in the time of the *Beis HaMikdash* wanted to fight when the right thing was to wait it out. So there are two sides: act or hold back, fight or run.

phrases.he: וכמו כל שיקול הדעת
phrases.en: and like every *shikul hadaas*

phrases.he: בא בהכרעה
ואחר הכרעה ישקול במאזני צדק שהן נצח והוד, איך להביא השפע למקבל כו'

blocks.text: Every *shikul hadaas* (weighing of the mind) ends in a decision; the whole middle line is weighing and judging. First you decide the *etzem*, good or bad; then again how to bring it out: the scales of *netzach* and *hod*, how the flow reaches the receiver.

sections.title: The middle line is one: it reaches the inner Keser, so it can join the two
sections.summary: *Daas*, *tiferes* and *yesod* are one middle line, like the long bar through the boards of the *Mishkan*: on each level a personal decision between two poles. It can join the lines because it goes up to the inner *Keser*, the goal for which both sides are only tools.

phrases.he: והיינו כללות ענין קו האמצעי דת''י, שמחבר לב' קוין דימין ושמאל

blocks.text: This is the middle line, *daas*, *tiferes* and *yesod*. *Yesod* connects *netzach* and *hod* by deciding out of a personal interest and connection. The real teacher relates to the student and tailors the thing for him, like *hashgacha pratis* (individual Divine providence). *Yesod* decides what is best between the two here.

So a *bar daas* (person of understanding) appreciates both sides and still makes a human, wise choice. People who give good advice see both sides, know where this person is holding and how each approach plays out, and what is best here. That is the middle line, connecting right and left.

phrases.he: ופרטי התכללותן נקרא י''ב גבולי אלכסון כידוע,
phrases.en: And the particular ways that they connect are called the twelve diagonal lines.

phrases.he: וקו האמצעי נקרא בריח התיכון
phrases.en: The middle line is called the support beam,

phrases.he: שמבריח מן הקצה כו'

blocks.title: The twelve edges of a cube
blocks.text: **The particular ways that they connect are called the twelve diagonal lines**, which can be counted two ways. One is a cube's twelve edges. From the middle of a cube you can go north, south, east, west, up and down: six, like the six *middos*. But you can also go diagonally, northeast or northwest, four on the compass, four up and four down: twelve.

The other, closer to the text: draw the *sefiros* as a *partzuf* in three lines. Seven lines join them up and down, three across, and twelve diagonally, which is how they include each other; the last two run from *bina* to *netzach* and from *chachma* to *hod*.

blocks.title: The middle bar of the Mishkan
blocks.text:
**The middle line is called the support beam**, the *bariach hatichon* (middle bar), which bolts from end to end, as a house's support beam runs all the way through. In the *Mishkan* each wall had two bars through rings outside, top and bottom, and through a hole drilled in the center of every board ran one long pole through all three walls.

Seen from the side, the right and left lines are separate for each wall, but the middle line runs through everything, the same. It is really one *inyan*.

*Daas*, *tiferes* and *yesod*, and also *Keser* and *Malchus*, are really one *sefira*, the middle line: your personal decision, in the intellect in *daas*, in the *middos* in *tiferes*, for *netzach* and *hod* in *yesod*. Each level has two poles, and your decision between them is the middle line.

blocks.title: The dimmer switch
blocks.text: Like a dimmer switch: there is all the way off and all the way on, and where you set it is the middle line.

phrases.he: דהיינו שעולה עד בחינת פנימית הכתר,
phrases.en: and that's the *inyan* that it goes all the way to *pnimiyus haKeser*,

phrases.he: שלמעלה מהתחלקות הקוין
על כן יש בכחו לחבר ולכלול ב' הקוין כו'.
phrases.en: therefore it's able to connect.

blocks.text: It goes all the way up to the *pnimiyus* of the *Keser*, which is why *davka* it can decide: it looks at what you really want to accomplish, and knowing where you are going, finds the best way there.

That is higher than the division into lines. From there *chesed* and *gevura* are *keilim* (vessels), "just a means to an end," and tied to the end you can find whatever compromise reaches it. So *Tikun* comes from higher than *Tohu*, from the *nekuda*, the *pnimiyus*: coming *b'etzem* (in essence), above the *hischalkus* (division), **therefore it's able to connect**.

sections.title: The inner Keser: the revealed will and delight, with a hidden reason
sections.summary: *Keser sheb'Keser* is the will and delight that come out revealed, with ten *sefiros* of their own. Its *chachma* is the *ta'am kamus*, the hidden reason for the will, really a taste of delight; its *middos* are unlimited, an impossible dream, and are called the days of old next to the *middos* of *chachma* and *bina*.

phrases.he: וביאור ענין פנימית הכתר דנאצלים שנקרא כתר שבכתר (והוא בחינת כתר דעתיק יומין ואריך אנפין כו')
היינו בחינת הרצון והתענוג הבא בגלוי,
phrases.en: It's like when you have a revealed desire and a revealed pleasure.

phrases.he: שנקרא אור הכתר,
שגם הוא כלול מעשר ספירות
phrases.en: that this is also has ten *sefiros*.

blocks.text: The *pnimiyus* of the *Keser* of *Atzilus*, the *Keser sheb'Keser*, is like the *Akudim* (bound lights), the single *nekuda* that includes everything: the revealed will and delight. It too has ten *sefiros*.

phrases.he: ובחינת חכמה שבכתר זהו הטעם לרצון
phrases.en: the *chachma* of the *Keser* is the reason for the *ratzon*.

phrases.he: ונקרא טעם כמוס לרצון

blocks.text: The *chachma* of the *Keser* is the reason for the will, called a *ta'am kamus* (hidden reason), here the reason that comes after the will. Rabbi Walters thinks it is called hidden because the will usually covers the reason: even the reason you give is not the real one.
Or it is hidden because the *pnimiyus* of *ta'am* is taste: the *geshmak* (relish), the special *taanug* (delight) you want it for.

blocks.title: Why that flavor ice cream?
blocks.text: So the form you find for your will is your reason. Ask a person why he picked that flavor of ice cream, and he says it is more chocolatey: that only tells you what it is. He wants a certain *geshmak*, and the reason only pinpoints which aspect he wants.

phrases.he: וכן יש בו חסד ונצח
phrases.en: and it also has *chesed* and *netzach*,

phrases.he: והכל בבחינת הרצון שהוא בלתי מוגבל,
phrases.en: and the *ratzon*, it's not limited.

phrases.he: גם שבא בגלוי מעצם העלם הרצון כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: It also has *chesed* and *netzach*, all in the will and all unlimited, though revealed out of the will's concealment. It has passed through *Adam Kadmon* and become a will for a particular thing, a house instead of a home, but it is still unlimited and unreasonable.

blocks.title: The impossible mansion
blocks.text: A house is realistic, something you could have. But in the *Keser* he wants an impossible mansion, a palace infinitely big and rich. So with everything: from the essential will a person's *chesed*, say his love for his child, is infinite; he wants to give infinitely.

phrases.he: ועל כן המדות שברצון ותענוג נקרא ימי קדם
phrases.en: that's why they're called the olden days.

phrases.he: לגבי מדות שבחכמה ובינה
phrases.en: compared to the *middos* that come in *chachma* and *bina*

phrases.he: שבאים בהגבלה כפי הגבלת השכל הגלוי בלבד
כמו שיתבאר,
phrases.en: like we'll explain,

phrases.he: עד בחינת מלכות שבכתר
phrases.en: until *Malchus sheb'Keser*.

blocks.text: So the *middos* in the will and delight are called *yemei kedem*, the olden days, like everything was bigger in the olden days, when you walked ten miles to school, uphill both ways. Maybe it is connected; he finds it interesting that they are called old.

Beside the *middos* in *chachma* and *bina*, which think what is practical, these are *kedem*, primal: your essential desire before you get practical, "your original dream," as the *ratzon kadum* (primordial will) is the days of old to *Adam Kadmon*. *Chachma* and *bina* bring it down to scale, to what the revealed intellect can do, down to *Malchus sheb'Keser*.

sections.title: Above the division: the will with no reason, and the curtain before it
sections.summary: The outer *Keser* divides into lines because a reason gives the will a form, with better and worse. The *Keser sheb'Keser* is a simple will with no reason, all or nothing, like G-d's "Be silent, so it arose in thought". The *paroches* between it and *chachma* is where the will takes a form, so prayer goes before it to change judgement to kindness.

phrases.he: ומבחינת חיצוניות דכתר נחלק לג' קוין
phrases.en: and from the *chitzoniyus* of the *Keser* though it already divides into three *kavin*.

phrases.he: מפני שבטעם הכמוס לרצון נקרא התחלקות הרצון לחסד וגבורה וממוצע כו'

blocks.text: But from the *chitzoniyus* of the *Keser* it already divides into three lines, because in the hidden reason *chesed*, *gevura* and a middle are recognizable. (He reads the text's *nikra*, "is called," as *nikar*, "is recognizable.")

Once you give what you want a *tzura* (form), a reason, there is better and worse, closer and farther, and *chachma* and *bina* look for what you can actually get that comes closest. So from the *chitzoniyus* it already has a form; even an impractical one, a huge mansion, can be met with the biggest thing we can find. From there a *Tikun* can decide on the three lines.

phrases.he: אבל בכתר שבכתר שלמעלה מטעם כמוס לרצון עדיין,
phrases.en: but the *Keser* *Keser* is higher than any particular *ratzon*,

phrases.he: רק רצון פשוט ועצמי בלא טעם כלל
כי אין טעם לרצון כלל, גם לא טעם כמוס

blocks.text: But the *Keser sheb'Keser* is above any particular will: a simple, essential will with no reason. The essential will has no compromise: your inner goal you either got or you didn't.
There is no reason for it at all: you want it because you want it. Once you work out that you want it like this, you have tied your essential will to a form.

blocks.title: The will for money and the get-rich-quick tapes
blocks.text: Relatively, take the will for money: in its *nekuda* it is essential, above every reason. Then in the *chitzoniyus* *chachma* and *bina* picture how to get it, a business deal, or one of the get-rich-quick tapes that gets you all psyched up. Even a totally impractical dream is already a particular way, already coming into a line.

He already sees some things as closer to what he wants and some farther, so the form has to fit the will. The essential will is not like that: simple and essential, with no reason in it at all, not even a hidden one.

phrases.he: כענין שתוק כך עלה במחשבה כו', וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר

blocks.text: As with "Be silent, so it arose in thought," said of the ten martyrs: no compromise there; that is what He wanted. A means to an end could be bettered; the thing itself cannot.

Like the *para aduma* (red heifer), "This is the statute of the Torah." In one explanation of the Rebbe, why an *aliya* (ascent) needs a *yerida* (descent) is the *chok* (a commandment kept just because G-d said so): why one becomes *tamei* (impure) to make another *tahor* (pure). That the world works so, we understand.

blocks.title: Profit and the sink
blocks.text: To make a profit you must invest; to fix your sink you get your hands dirty. That is the way it works.

blocks.question: Why did G-d have to make it that way?
blocks.text: G-d did not have to make it no pain, no gain; He could have given us all the virtues. The explanations say *nahama d'kisufa* (the bread of shame), but He could have given the virtue without it. That is the *chok*: G-d chose it so. That is the real essential will and delight, the fiftieth gate, the essential thing beyond description, as explained elsewhere.

phrases.he: על כן הוא למעלה מהתחלקות ימין ושמאל כו', הגם שבא בגלוי מבחינת האחרונה שבהעלם הרצון דבחינת אדם קדמון (כנזכר לעיל בסוף אות י''ט)

blocks.question: "Wait a minute, but it already has an order from *Adam Kadmon*. *Adam Kadmon* already makes three lines."
blocks.text: So it is above right and left, though it comes out revealed from the last level of *Adam Kadmon*'s concealed will. Take money: in *Adam Kadmon* you already made three lines working out your self-image, and from the essential desire to be happy came a picture of prosperity, of which being rich is a part. So it is already divided.

True, against the essential will before *Adam Kadmon* it became lines. But once it comes out, to what follows it is an essential will again, *gilui ha'helem* (revelation of what is hidden), the essence tied to this thing, with its full force while that holds. You want happiness; if your *Adam Kadmon* says happiness is money, you want money, *nekuda*, as they say in Hebrew, and that is not negotiable.

That is how a Jew can have *mesirus nefesh* for a *mitzva* (commandment). What he really wants is to be connected to G-d. Were a prophet to tell you to transgress any *mitzva*, it would be a *mitzva* to do it; so you do not essentially want to keep Shabbos, and if a prophet said so, or in *pikuach nefesh* (danger to life), it is a *mitzva* to desecrate it.

How, then, can a Jew have *mesirus nefesh* when a *goy* says he will shoot him unless he is *mechalel Shabbos*? Where the Torah says this connects him to G-d, it carries the full force of his will to be connected; where it says it does not, he can do it and stay connected. Once the two are tied, the full force of his *yechida* (the essence of the soul) is in every deed, totally non-negotiable: the essential will, not the three *mochin*.

sensitivity.reason: Uses the word goy for the non-Jew who threatens a Jew, a word many readers take as dismissive; the series flags the word wherever it occurs.
sensitivity.publishable: How, then, can a Jew have *mesirus nefesh* when a non-Jew says he will shoot him unless he is *mechalel Shabbos*? Where the Torah says this connects him to G-d, it carries the full force of his will to be connected; where it says it does not, he can do it and stay connected. Once the two are tied, the full force of his *yechida* (the essence of the soul) is in every deed, totally non-negotiable: the essential will, not the three *mochin*.

phrases.he: ועל זה אמר והבדילה הפרוכת בין הקדש כו'
phrases.en: the *paroches* separates between the *Kodesh* and the *Kodesh Kodashim*,

phrases.he: בחינת פרסא שבין כתר דכתר לחכמה כו'
והוא בחינת קרומא דאוירא
phrases.en: This is the membrane of air, the arachnoid membrane in the brain, it's called,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב במקום אחר באריכות

blocks.text: Of this it says, "The *paroches* (the curtain) shall separate between the Holy" and the Holy of Holies: between the *Keser* of *Keser*, the essential will, and the *chachma* of the will, where it has a form. There is a *masach* (screen), the *parsa* (partition), between them.

It is the *kruma d'avira*, the membrane of air, in the brain the arachnoid membrane, as written at length elsewhere; chapter 25 will discuss it, with the hairs, *Atik*, and the thirteen *tikunim* of the beard of *Arich*.

blocks.title: The fluid of delight under the skull
blocks.text: Physically, a liquid under the skull, in medicine, he thinks, the subdural fluid, is the essential delight, giving a person the essential feeling of delight and will. It does not come down pure: a spongy membrane holds it, and little hair-like tubes inject it into the brain. An active part of the brain draws more of it and is stimulated; dripping on the back of the spine, it gives delight.

sensitivity.reason: Says a fluid under the skull is the source of delight, injected into the brain and dripping on the spine, as medical fact; not what medicine says, and a reader may take it as fact.
sensitivity.publishable: The essential delight does not come down pure: a membrane holds it, and wherever a faculty is active, it draws more of the delight and is stimulated.

blocks.title: Each person's membrane, each person's nature
blocks.text: It drips by the shape of the membrane, and each person's is a little different. That gives a person his nature: he enjoys certain things more and is better at them, because certain parts of his brain, certain forms, get delight more easily. That is the *mazal* (lit. a flow), the *mazalos*, from *nozel*, flowing, for chapter 25.

sensitivity.reason: Continues the physiology of the brain fluid, making the shape of the membrane the cause of a person's nature, as medical fact.
sensitivity.publishable: It comes through by the shape of the membrane, and each person's is a little different. That gives a person his nature: he enjoys certain things more and is better at them, because certain forms get delight more easily. That is the *mazal* (lit. a flow), the *mazalos*, from *nozel*, flowing, for chapter 25.

blocks.text: So this *masach* is what connects: to go from the essential will to the means, you must make something that ties the essential will to a form, as written at length elsewhere.

phrases.he: ועל כן אומר יהי רצון מלפניך, מלפני הפרסא כו'
לשנות מרצון של דין לרצון של חסד וכהאי גוונא כו' ודי למבין:

blocks.text: So one says, "May it be the will before You," before the *parsa*. Wanting something changed, we connect *davka* to the essential will, above any form, where it can come out in any form and G-d can do the same thing another way. Once through the *paroches* it is set in a form, already a reason for the will.

To change a will of *din* to one of *chesed*, and this is enough for one who understands: *davka* the essential will, the essence of the *Keser*, can go either way. That is the *inyan* of the three *mochin*.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does *chachma* lean towards *chesed* and *bina* towards *gevura*? Use the gift and the person who is "just misguided".
Why is *netzach* "separate" from *chesed*, and what does *mivtzaim* in the cold show about it?
What does *daas* do with the two ways of looking at a person, and why can a computer not do it?
How is *tiferes* like mercy after the verdict, and what is the attribute of Yaakov?
Why can the middle line join the two lines, and what does the middle bar of the *Mishkan* show about it?
Why is there no compromise in the *Keser sheb'Keser*, and why does prayer go "before the *parsa*"?

notes.text: Line 27: he reads "it is Keser of Adam Kadmon" (79 w1465-1477) where the text has "Keser of Atik Yomin and Arich Anpin"; and in line 28 he reads "which is called Arich Anpin" (79 w1494-1502) where the text has "called the light of the Keser". The block follows the chapter's text and his explanation (the Akudim, the single nekuda) without naming either reading.
Line 34: he reads the text's nikra as nikar ("recognizable") and says it is "supposed to be" so (79 w2223-2241); the block says so. The transcript hears the two words the same and is garbled here.

The physiology in classes 78 (the kidney and adrenal glands, adrenaline and testosterone, 78 w2122-2423) and 80 (a fluid under the skull, which he calls subdural, as the essential delight dripping on the spine, 80 w1368-1606) is kept as he gave it, with his own hedges ("from what I researched", "I think"). It is loose as anatomy (the adrenal glands are not two glands stacked on the kidney; the subdural space normally holds no fluid; the fluid around the brain is cerebrospinal fluid, under the arachnoid). Those blocks are flagged health-or-legal, as chapter 15 flags his medical claims, with publishable texts that keep the hod/netzach and the membrane points.

Phrases he reads without translating keep their Hebrew alone: the start of line 1, line 2 up to Keser sheb'Keser (he explains it instead), the end of line 3 and all of line 4, the end of line 7 (b'davar murkav, which he glosses as "not an etzem chesed"), the end of line 8, the end of line 9, the start of lines 11 and 13, lines 14, 16 and 23 (read whole, then explained), most of line 15 and line 19, the middle of line 20, the end of line 21, line 22, the end of line 24, the end of line 25, line 27 and the middle of line 28, the end of line 29 and of line 31, the middle of line 32, line 34, the end of line 35, all of line 36 (his "why do you want it? You want it because you want it" explains it rather than translating it), lines 37 and 38, line 40, the end of line 41, and lines 42-43. The English of line 13 ("it's davka the middle thing, which is daas", 78 w366-373) is from his summary after the opening question; the end of line 12 (78 w6-14) is from class 78's opening, and the English of the end of line 20 is from class 79's opening (79 w11-20). The English of line 26 is the end of the sentence right after his reading of it (79 w1460-1464); the first half of that sentence ("since it's coming from b'etzem, it's higher than this hischalkus") gives the reason and belongs to line 25, so it is in the block, not the phrase.

In the mesirus nefesh block (80 w1142-1176) the transcript has "the whole inyan of shin-samech-heh kedushos", which is garbled (perhaps the 365 prohibitions); the block keeps only his point that the Torah tells a Jew where a deed is not connected to his connection to G-d.

"Be silent, so it arose in thought" (line 37): he ties it to the ten martyrs of the kingdom (80 w388-416); the Gemara (Menachos 29b) says it of Rabbi Akiva's death, one of the ten. The block keeps his words. "That is here the fiftieth gate" (80 w717-737) is kept as he said it; the transcript has "sha'ar nun".

The goy in the halachic case of being forced to desecrate Shabbos (80 w1079-1106) is flagged other-groups, as the series flags the word wherever it occurs (chapters 15, 17, 18, 28); the publishable text says "a non-Jew", which keeps the halachic case. The remark itself is neutral, so an editor may decide the word can stand.
